title: Luther's barber
hook: Luther taught his barber to pray through the Lord's Prayer, Commandments and Creed like a garland

segments.voice: Yesterday, common prayer: one collect, the same words, said together. Your line was prayer in common. Whose words stood in for yours? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-seven.

A man who cuts hair for a living asks his customer a question that can be hard to ask out loud: how do you actually pray? The customer is Martin Luther. The story goes that Luther answered with a little book, written for, in his words, a good friend, Master Peter the barber. In English it's called A Simple Way to Pray. A famous reformer, writing a how-to for a man with a razor. Today the path moves on from the Anglican prayer book to the Lutheran and Reformed ways, and it starts in a barbershop. Today: Luther's barber.

Luther starts with honesty. He admits there are days his heart is cold and he has no wish to pray. On those days he takes his little psalter, goes to his room, or to church if people are there, and begins saying, quietly, the Ten Commandments, the Creed, the Lord's Prayer and some psalms, the way a child would. Words he already knows by heart. Then he slows down inside them. He takes one commandment at a time and makes of it a garland of four strands. First, instruction: what does this teach me? Second, thanksgiving: what can I thank God for here? Third, confession: where have I fallen short? Fourth, prayer: what do I ask? Take the first commandment: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." Instruction: God asks to be trusted above everything. Thanks: that God offers to be my God at all. Confession: the other things I lean on harder. Prayer: help me trust you. Then Luther turns to Peter's own trade. A good barber, he says, keeps his whole mind on the razor and the hair. If he chats and looks around and thinks of other things, he may cut someone's mouth, or nose, or throat. Prayer needs the whole heart in the same way. And then comes a surprising freedom. If, partway through, a thought catches fire, Luther says, let the rest go and listen. In his words, the Holy Spirit himself is preaching, and that sermon is worth far more than our own prayers. So the method is a trellis, not a cage. It's there to get a cold heart started, and Luther is glad to see it climbed over.

Here's the practice: one commandment, four strands. Sit and let your breath settle. Take "Thou shalt not steal," or go back to the first one. Give each strand a few breaths. What does it teach? What is there to be thankful for in it? Where have I missed it? What would I ask? If you pray, speak the four strands to God. If you don't, let the four questions turn over quietly. And if one thought takes hold, follow it, the way Luther told Peter to. The bell holds the time.
Luther's barber. Master Peter, for whom Luther wrote a simple way to pray: the Commandments, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer, woven into garlands of four strands.

Your line: a simple way to pray. Today, when you're doing something with your hands, cutting, typing, chopping, keep your whole mind on it for one minute, the way Luther's barber kept his on the razor. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Lutherans and other Christians use Luther's method, praying slowly through a commandment, a line of the Creed or a petition of the Lord's Prayer as instruction, thanksgiving, confession and prayer.

options: finish the method first; the thought can wait.
let the plan go and listen.
fork.reveal: Luther says to let the rest go and listen, because the Holy Spirit is preaching. the method is there to warm a cold heart, not to fence it in.

trapdoor: what you thought: a barber who picked up a prayer from a famous customer.
what it means: Luther's simple way: say the Commandments, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer slowly, and weave each part into a garland of four strands.
what a scholar hears: the four strands are instruction, thanksgiving, confession and prayer, and Luther tells Peter to drop the scheme when the Spirit begins to preach.

notes: The whole of Luther's teaching is paraphrased from A Simple Way to Pray (Eine einfältige Weise zu beten); no English translation is quoted. Confirm: the cold-heart opening and the little psalter; saying the Commandments, Creed, Lord's Prayer and psalms 'as a child'; the 'garland of four strands' (instruction, thanksgiving, confession, prayer); the barber who keeps his mind on the razor or cuts mouth, nose or throat; and letting the scheme go when the Holy Spirit 'preaches'.

'The story goes that Luther answered with a little book': that Peter Beskendorf asked Luther how to pray is the usual account; the book's dedication to 'a good friend, Master Peter the barber' is in the text. Year and Peter's later history are deliberately left out.

'His word is worth far more than our own' softens Luther's comparison (often rendered 'one word of his sermon is far better than a thousand of our prayers'), because the exact number could not be checked here.
'Saying, quietly' paraphrases Luther saying the texts to himself; confirm.
The hook marks the move from the Anglican section to 'The Lutheran and Reformed ways' (days 1157–1162 in the outline).
Original is null: the key words are German, not a biblical language, and the German for 'garland' could not be verified.

Editor pass: 'a question plenty of people never dare to ask' (unsourced claim about people) softened; 'the great argument of the Reformation was raging' (unsourced history) cut, and the doubled 'Today' in the hook fixed; 'The Holy Spirit is preaching' now attributed to Luther rather than asserted by the narrator; garbled myth reveal ('admits days his heart was cold') repaired.
Audit (2026-10-02): hook transition 'the Anglican rooms give way to the Lutheran and Reformed ones' was garbled; rewritten plainly.
